p.title: Campaign Contributions Facilitate Access to Congressional Officials: A Randomized Field Experiment

ext.title: Campaign Contributions Facilitate Access to Congressional Officials: A Randomized Field Experiment
ext.venue: American Journal of Political Science, Vol. 60, No. 3 (July 2016), pp. 545-558 (copyright 2015, Midwest Political Science Association). Metadata hint corrected: full author names and venue added.
ext.document_type: Journal article; empirical; randomized field experiment with one randomization-inference analysis and an ordered probit robustness check
ext.coverage: Full text read in chunks: all lines of the extraction (1-1349), covering abstract, introduction, theory, design, randomization, implementation, protocol, results, Table 1, discussion, references, and the supporting-information index. Page locations were inferred from the running page-number markers in the extraction. Supporting Tables S1 (response rules) and S2 (covariate balance) are referenced but not present in the text file, so they are not reviewed. Paul's markup: no markup files were supplied (the task listed none), so paul_markup is empty.
ext.research_question: Can an interest group obtain superior access to senior congressional officials because its members have donated to political campaigns? Put as a counterfactual: would House offices have treated the same group members differently had the offices not known they were donors? (p.545, p.548)
ext.theory: Campaign contributions may buy access through quid pro quo exchange, expected future donations, forestalling donations to rivals, and signals of ideology, expertise or preference intensity; access is a precondition for influence and legislators' time is finite. Observational work is confounded by shared ideology, and contributors may give to legislators who already support them or to those whose support is in doubt. (pp.546-548)
ext.data: Unit: congressional office (district scheduler contacted by e-mail). Sample: every U.S. House representative of one party who had not already cosponsored the bill, 191 offices after one of an original 192 was dropped because of a misdirected e-mail (fn 5, p.549). Recruited attendees: around a dozen CREDO Action members per district who had previously donated to campaigns (p.549). Organization: CREDO Action, a liberal political organization with about 3.5 million members (p.549). Period: implementation June, July and August 2013 (p.551). Bill: a measure to ban a chemical; no vote was held (p.549, p.554). Per-arm counts are not reported in the text; the design implies 64 Revealed Donor offices (one per block) and 127 Constituent offices, which matches the Table 1 percentages (derived, not stated). Party is not named in the text.
ext.method: Blocked randomized field experiment. Offices were blocked into 64 triplets using blockTools (Mahalanobis distance) on six covariates; one office per block randomly assigned to Revealed Donor and two to Constituent (pp.549-550). The request e-mail described attendees as "local campaign donors" (Revealed Donor) or "local constituents" (Constituent); nothing else varied, and correspondence was standardized by a prespecified protocol (pp.550-551). Outcome: the rank of the official who would attend, recorded more than 24 hours in advance and confirmed after the meeting, coded into six ordered categories by two coders blind to assignment (p.552). Analysis: exact p-values from randomization inference under the sharp null, one comparison per cumulative rank; Bonferroni check across five comparisons; ordered probit with randomization-inference p-value as an omnibus test (pp.552-554).
ext.identification: Identification rests on random assignment of offices to the donor-label versus constituent-label condition, within covariate blocks, so covariates (balance omnibus p=.92, chi-square 1.44, 5 df, p.550) and chance differences in official availability are balanced by design. The randomized treatment is the donor status of attendees as revealed to the office, not actual contributions; this is a "mechanism experiment" that approximates randomizing donor status (fn 4, p.548). Donors' actual giving was not randomized and no deception occurred: the meetings were real, attendees knew donations might be disclosed, and the requests asked for nothing illegal (p.551). The design does not establish that the label operates through quid pro quo rather than the other mechanisms listed under theory.
ext.scope: Population: U.S. House offices of one party that had not cosponsored one bill, one advocacy group, one set of meetings. Institution: House district offices and their schedulers, not Senate or committee-level access. Era: 2013, after Citizens United (2010); the paper frames findings against Citizens United and McCutcheon v. FEC (p.556). Generalization to corporate or wealthy donors and to other contexts is explicitly untested (p.555).

key_findings.finding: Senior access rose when the donor label was revealed: chief of staff or above was available in 12.5% of Revealed Donor offices vs 2.4% of Constituent offices (cumulative), p=.006 by randomization inference.
Legislative director or deputy chief of staff or above: 18.8% vs 5.5% (cumulative), p=.005. The text describes this as more than a threefold increase.
Member of Congress meetings: 7.8% vs 2.4%, p=.07. Not significant at .05 on its own, though the text describes it as more than three times as likely.

Abstract summary: senior policy makers were available between three and four times more often when the donor label was revealed. Ratios implied by Table 1 are about 3.2x (Member), 3.4x (LD or above), 5.2x (chief of staff or above).

Lower-ranked staff showed no reliable difference: DC-based legislative assistant or local district director cumulative 37.5% vs 30.7%, p=.17; other district-based staffer cumulative 48.4% vs 43.3%, p=.26.

Any meeting: the text says 56.7% of Constituent and 51.6% of Revealed Donor offices scheduled any meeting, and that about half of offices granted meetings overall. Table 1 instead labels 56.7% and 51.6% as 'No Meeting', which reverses the text's meaning. The table columns sum to 100% under the 'No Meeting' reading, so the text wording looks inconsistent with the table.
key_findings.location: Text p.552 and p.553 (lines on 'scheduled any meeting'); Table 1 p.552

key_findings.finding: Ordered probit across the six ranks, with randomization-inference p-value: overall effect of the donor label on access level, p=.05.

Senior comparisons (chief of staff and above; LD and above) remain significant after a conservative Bonferroni correction across five comparisons at the .05 level; the text reports ps < .01 for these two.
Cosponsorship outcome: only nine legislators cosponsored during the study, with the same share in both conditions. The low base rate makes this uninformative about access effects on cosponsorship.

limitations: One experiment cannot establish which mechanism (quid pro quo, expected future donations, expertise, preference intensity, prognostic value of donors) produces the effect; the authors call mechanism 'ripe for future research' (p.555).
The treatment is a label in a meeting request, not actual donations; the 'revealed donor' cue could also signal that the group cared more about the issue (fn 4, p.548).
The design compares donors with constituents only; all offices were told attendees were constituents, so the relative importance of being a constituent versus a contributor is not measured (p.555).

Access is not influence; the study does not show whether greater access changes policy outcomes (p.555-556). Cosponsorship results are too imprecise and may reflect outreach, not the meetings (p.553).
Single organization (CREDO Action), single bill, one party's House members who had not cosponsored, and one three-month window (June-August 2013); replication in other settings is needed (p.555).
Staffers may have read the donor label as meaning group members had given to that legislator, which the authors note (p.550).
Table 1 'No Meeting' figures conflict with the text's 'scheduled any meeting' wording (p.552-553).
Per-arm sample sizes are not reported in the text; the 64/127 split is derived from the design. The 192-to-191 reduction is explained in fn 5 (p.549).
Supporting Tables S1 and S2 are not in the text file, so the covariate balance and response rules are cited but not checked.
The abstract's 'three and four times' summary understates the ratio for chief of staff or above (about 5.2x by Table 1 arithmetic).

measures: Access outcome: rank of the official attending (Member of Congress; chief of staff; legislative director or deputy CoS; DC legislative assistant or local district director; other district staffer; no meeting), recorded more than 24 hours in advance and confirmed after the meeting
Cumulative probability of access at or above each rank, by condition (Table 1)

Covariates for blocking and balance: ProgressivePunch environment score, cosponsorship of the same bill in a previous congress, years in Congress, ideology (Clinton-Jackman-Rivers ideal points), donor members within 40 miles of the district office, Barack Obama's 2012 two-party vote share in the district
Cosponsorship of the bill during the study period (nine total)
Treatment: revealed donor status (local campaign donors vs local constituents) in the meeting request

short_quotes.quote: senior policy makers made themselves available between three and four times more often

rel.summary_md:
Kalla and Broockman ran a blocked randomized field experiment in 2013. CREDO Action asked 191 House offices for a district meeting about a chemical-ban bill. All offices belonged to one party and none had cosponsored the bill. In one office per covariate-matched triplet (64 offices, a number derived from the design), the request called the attendees "local campaign donors". The other 127 offices were told "local constituents", and nothing else changed. The outcome was the rank of the most senior official who attended. Over June to August 2013, a chief of staff or more senior official attended in 12.5% of donor-label offices and 2.4% of constituent-label offices (p=.006). For legislative director or above the figures were 18.8% and 5.5% (p=.005), and for the Member personally 7.8% and 2.4% (p=.07). Lower-ranked staff showed no reliable difference (48.4% vs 43.3% at any district staffer or above, p=.26). The ordered probit gave p=.05.

The randomized treatment was the donor label, not real money. The paper cannot say why the label works, and it measures access, not influence. Only 9 offices cosponsored during the study, so the cosponsorship comparison tells us nothing.

For Paul's systems, the paper mainly bounds an existing citation. flip_model.py:21 cites Kalla and Broockman for "money buys access/effort > votes" and labels the 0.35/0.65 money/peer split CALIBRATED. The paper supports the access half of that line. It says nothing about votes, positions, cosponsorship or the money-to-peer ratio, so it cannot calibrate those constants.

The paper's best transferable idea is its outcome measure: the seniority of the official who takes the meeting. The prospective contract and the staffer routes have no outcome of that kind. The contract scores new cosponsorships, which is the same low-base-rate outcome that left this paper uninformative. Nothing here supports the competitiveness multiplier.

bearings.paper_claim: Revealing donor status raised senior access 3 to 5 times: chief of staff or above 12.5% vs 2.4% (p=.006); LD or above 18.8% vs 5.5% (p=.005); Member 7.8% vs 2.4% (p=.07). Only 9 of 191 offices cosponsored, at equal shares in both arms, which is too few to say anything about positions or votes.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 p.552; text pp.553-554; fn 11 p.553
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b) puts a saturating CU-money term (weight WM 0.35) directly into a member's probability of flipping on a topic, against a peer term (WP 0.65). The constant line cites Kalla & Broockman as part of the basis for 'CALIBRATED: money is the minority partner ... money buys access/effort > votes'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper backs only the qualitative claim that donor status opens doors at senior levels. It gives no estimate of WM/WP, HALFF or the receipts-relative saturation, and no effect on votes or positions. It also randomized a label rather than dollars, used one liberal group, one bill and one party, and ran June to August 2013. The citation therefore supports the ordering 'access before votes', not any number in pflip. The CALIBRATED tag should cite this paper as qualitative support only.

bearings.paper_claim: Measured as the seniority of the official who attends, the donor label had detectable effects in 191 offices over 3 months. Measured as cosponsorship, it was uninformative: 9 cosponsors in total, at equal shares in both arms.
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 p.552; fn 11 p.553; outcome coding p.552
bearings.system_side: H1 correlates frozen seed_prob (Spearman) with new cosponsorship count deltas. It requires at least 60 days and at least 150 members with any cosponsorship delta. The F5 replay found 72 of 511 new-event members, which is underpowered.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transfer is about outcome choice, not effect size. Cosponsorship after contact is a rare event in a field experiment as well as in Paul's panel. A second contract whose outcome is the seniority of the official met, recorded from a real outreach log, would accumulate events faster. It would need an outreach log, which the system does not have, and its own pre-registered look under the single-look rule. Any such result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Who asks changes which tier of staff takes the meeting. The donor label moved senior access (chief of staff or above, 12.5% vs 2.4%) but not access to district staff (48.4% vs 43.3%, p=.26). The office's scheduler decides who meets.
bearings.system_side: The router returns the least-cost introduction route to staff anchored at a member office. A member-context prestige modifier (MEMBER_BETA) is applied as a bonus and is explicitly not access evidence. Route costs are heuristic outputs, not access probabilities (D-025).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports recording the seniority of the person reached as the validation target for routes, matching its six-rank coding. It does not justify converting route costs or ranks into access probabilities. That would break D-025, and the paper measured a requester attribute, not a co-worker tie. Its setting is constituent meetings in district offices, not warm introductions through former colleagues.

bearings.paper_claim: When an organized group tells an office that its constituents are campaign donors, senior staff and the Member make themselves available 3 to 5 times more often than for constituents alone.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.545; Table 1 p.552; limitations p.555
bearings.system_side: Sphere of Influence = 0.45 giving + 0.45 volunteering + 0.10 household. Giving = (charitable donor + cpi_donor)/4 + contrib_high/2. The weights are a 'leaning' ruling, and the scale assumes givers engage members.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is relevant only to campaign-donor status, and only when the donor status is made known to the office, as in an organized group's meeting request. It says nothing about charitable giving, and the config does not say what kind of giving contrib_high covers. It also says nothing about individuals acting alone or about volunteering. The evidence comes from one liberal organization in 2013. Use it to justify revealing donor status in the asks a CU league organizes, not to reweight the SOI giving term.

bearings.paper_claim: Offices were blocked on Obama's 2012 district vote share among six covariates (balance omnibus p=.92). The paper reports no effect heterogeneity by seat competitiveness.
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + exp(-max(lean,0)/5) multiplies the effective dollars on both money legs. AMPLITUDE and SCALE are uncalibrated judgment calls, and the reciprocity they encode is NOT validated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Blocking on district partisanship balances it across arms. It does not estimate whether the donor effect is larger in competitive seats, and with 64 treated offices the design could not have estimated that. The paper gives no support for c, and the multiplier stays unvalidated (D-104..D-108).

bearings.paper_claim: Access, not position change, was the measured effect. Cosponsorship (9 offices in total, equal shares) gives no evidence either way.
bearings.system_side: MAXSHIFT was cut from 40 to 18 on the premise that 'money moves POSITIONS little (buys access/effort, not votes)'. LOSSFRAME 1.10 makes competitor spending a loss frame.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper agrees with the framing but cannot be cited as a null effect on positions, because its cosponsorship estimate is uninformative rather than null. It does not bear on MAXSHIFT, HALF, DTHRESH or LOSSFRAME.

gaps_exposed: No measure of access in any component: nothing records which tier of official (Member, chief of staff, LD, LA, district staff) actually took a meeting. That is the outcome that responded to treatment in this paper.

No outreach or contact log, so the staffer routes and the H1 seed_prob contract have no direct contact outcome. Cosponsorship deltas are a rare-event stand-in, which is why F5 found 72 of 511 new-event members.

The engine has no access stage between money and position. The flip family maps dollars straight into pflip, so the step the paper actually demonstrates (money to access) is not represented separately from the step it does not test (access to position).
No estimate of how the donor-access effect varies with seat competitiveness. The competitiveness multiplier assumes such variation without evidence.
flags: The annotation is mislabeled. Paul's annotation record for this citation says its text is actually Furnas et al., so no Paul takeaway can be attributed to Kalla & Broockman until it is re-linked.

Citation over-reach in code. fec/engine/flip_model.py:21 lists Kalla & Broockman among the sources behind 'CALIBRATED' WM/WP 0.35/0.65. The paper supports only the qualitative claim that access comes before votes, and calibrates no constant.

Quote figures with their windows and denominators: 64 Revealed Donor vs 127 Constituent offices (derived from the design, not stated), one party's non-cosponsors, June to August 2013. The abstract's '3 to 4 times' understates the chief-of-staff ratio, which is about 5.2x by Table 1 arithmetic. Table 1's 'No Meeting' label contradicts the text's 'scheduled any meeting' (56.7% vs 51.6%).
These are access rates measured in the experiment. Do not carry them over as access or introduction probabilities for graph routes or ranks (D-025).
Do not use this paper to support the competitiveness multiplier. Reciprocity remains NOT validated (D-104..D-108).
rel.paul_alignment: The evidence matches Paul's position as summarized for the flip model: money buys access, and the model's 'money buys access, not votes' stance is consistent with the sources. It is a randomized test of the access half only. It does not support his ROI enthusiasm, the money weight in pflip, or any effect on positions. Paul's annotation record for this paper is stale or misfiled, since the stored text belongs to Furnas et al., so his notes have no takeaway of their own for Kalla & Broockman. The code already cites the paper (flip_model.py:21) more strongly than the paper can bear.

related.why: A survey experiment on congressional staff about money and information. Together with this field experiment on office access, it splits the 'money signals vs money buys' mechanism question that Kalla & Broockman leave open.
Kim et al. find observational donation-then-lobbying sequences. This paper randomizes the donor signal at the point of contact, giving causal support for the access step those sequences assume.
Low overlap between organizations' lobbying and PAC spending limits how often a donor label is actually available to lobbying actors, which bounds how far this result transfers to the FEC-LDA bridge.
A review of empirical lobbying and access models in which this experiment is a standard identification reference for the access channel.
Both frame campaign-money effects against Citizens United. Blackwell addresses confounding in observational money effects, which this paper avoids by randomization.
Bonica shows that donors are old and wealthy. That bears on who can credibly present as a 'donor' in Terrier-style organized asks, whereas the experiment's donors were CREDO members.
Holyoke treats lobbyist relationships as built on mutual need, and the experiment shows one need, the donor signal, shifting which staff tier engages.

paul_entries.citation: Kalla, Joshua L., and David E. Broockman. “Campaign contributions facilitate access to Congressional officials: A randomized field experiment.” American Journal of Political Science, vol. 60, no. 3, 2 Apr. 2015, pp. 545–558, https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12180.
paul_entries.text:
Kalla, Joshua L., and David E. Broockman. “Campaign contributions facilitate access to Congressional officials: A randomized field experiment.” *American Journal of Political Science*, vol. 60, no. 3, 2 Apr. 2015, pp. 545–558, [https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12180](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12180).

This article by Professors Furnas, LaPira, and others explores how the identity of a political information giver affects the recipient's receptiveness to that information in the context of legislative advocacy. By using a novel survey of 400 federal congressional staffers, where the identity of the individual or interest, the nature of the request, and the source of the statistics for said recommendation are provided, the authors reveal an “*epistemic closure among partisan staffers*.” They make clear their recommendation that an interest group should base its findings on evidence from a think tank that is ideologically aligned with the office it is engaging with. Put simply, the staffers want to hear only what they want to hear, will be psychologically averse to institutions they perceive as against their interests, and will be hesitant towards groups they perceive as pursuing their own goals. The implications of these findings are profound and can be seen as an explanation for the donation behavior of large dark-money funds. By channeling funds toward the building of ideological infrastructure, such groups are not recruiting their own champions, but cultivating them. Finally, regarding the current research, allocating venture capital funds to the growth of industry-aligned think tanks should be considered, scouted, and ultimately incorporated into future allocation models.
